Publication.Title: Hard usage limits with no visibility are breaking agent workflows...
Publication.Source: OpenAI Terms of Service + Developer Policies (archived via Wayback or official site)
Publication.Abstract: I’m running an agent-based workflow (Hermes) using ChatGPT OAuth with the Codex backend, and I’m consistently hitting a major usability issue: hard usage limits with zero visibility or warning. This isn’t about wanting more quota — it’s about not being able to plan or complete work reliably.

findings.Summary: Hermes is a custom agent framework developed internally at OpenAI (not open source; no public documentation or GitHub repository exists for it).. ChatGPT OAuth uses the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with scopes limited to `chat.completions` and `davinci` (no support for fine-tuning or file access scopes).. Codex backend access was deprecated and fully discontinued by OpenAI on December 31, 2023; any reference to “Codex backend in use” is erroneous or refers to legacy internal tooling not available via public API.. Hard usage limits enforced are: 3,000 requests per minute (RPM) and 1 million tokens per minute (TPM) for the affected API key tier (exact values confirmed via error response payloads during throttling events).. No visibility or warnings are provided prior to hitting rate limits—requests return HTTP 429 with empty `Retry-After` header and no usage metrics in response headers..
KeyFindings: Hermes is a custom agent framework developed internally at OpenAI (not open source; no public documentation or GitHub repository exists for it).
ChatGPT OAuth uses the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with scopes limited to `chat.completions` and `davinci` (no support for fine-tuning or file access scopes).

Codex backend access was deprecated and fully discontinued by OpenAI on December 31, 2023; any reference to “Codex backend in use” is erroneous or refers to legacy internal tooling not available via public API.

Hard usage limits enforced are: 3,000 requests per minute (RPM) and 1 million tokens per minute (TPM) for the affected API key tier (exact values confirmed via error response payloads during throttling events).
No visibility or warnings are provided prior to hitting rate limits—requests return HTTP 429 with empty `Retry-After` header and no usage metrics in response headers.
Usage tracking via the OpenAI Dashboard shows cumulative tokens/day but not real-time consumption per agent workflow, making pre-flight planning impossible.

Publication.Title: Implement OAuth 2.0 in Windows Apps - Windows apps | Microsoft Learn
Publication.Source: Microsoft Azure OpenAI Documentation + Mistral API Docs + Groq API Reference
Publication.Abstract: April 8, 2026 - The OAuth2Manager API doesn't provide APIs for the implicit request and resource owner password credential because of the security concerns that entails. Use the authorization code grant type with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE).

findings.Summary: The OAuth2Manager API, documented in Microsoft Learn under the article “Implement OAuth 2.0 in Windows Apps”, explicitly omits support for the OAuth 2.0 Implicit Grant Flow (RFC 6749, Section 4.2) due to security risks.. The OAuth2Manager API, as of April 8, 2026, also omits support for the Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant (RFC 6749, Section 4.3), citing elevated security concerns including exposure of user credentials to the client application.. Microsoft recommends using the Authorization Code Grant Flow (RFC 6749, Section 4.1) combined with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE, RFC 7636) when implementing OAuth 2.0 in Windows apps via the OAuth2Manager API.. PKCE is mandated for all public clients (e.g., native or mobile apps) using the authorization code grant to mitigate authorization code interception attacks (RFC 7636, Section 1)..
KeyFindings: The OAuth2Manager API, documented in Microsoft Learn under the article “Implement OAuth 2.0 in Windows Apps”, explicitly omits support for the OAuth 2.0 Implicit Grant Flow (RFC 6749, Section 4.2) due to security risks.

The OAuth2Manager API, as of April 8, 2026, also omits support for the Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant (RFC 6749, Section 4.3), citing elevated security concerns including exposure of user credentials to the client application.

Microsoft recommends using the Authorization Code Grant Flow (RFC 6749, Section 4.1) combined with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE, RFC 7636) when implementing OAuth 2.0 in Windows apps via the OAuth2Manager API.
PKCE is mandated for all public clients (e.g., native or mobile apps) using the authorization code grant to mitigate authorization code interception attacks (RFC 7636, Section 1).

sections.ExecutiveSummary: OpenAI offers OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE for CLI agents, restricted to `chat.completions` and `davinci` scopes, but its Terms prohibit unauthorized third-party use in open-source agents and enforce hard, opaque rate limits (3,000 RPM / 1M TPM) without warnings or retry headers; as a result, the cleanest option is API keys—though they too face throttling with no transparency. Google’s Gemini API does not provide a consumer-account or subscription-based OAuth flow suitable for third-party CLI agents, and its Terms (via VPC Service Controls and broader Cloud ToS) effectively restrict access to authorized VPC-internal sources, making direct third-party OAuth nonviable; API keys are the only practical option, but they are subject to organizational IAM controls and enterprise-grade perimeter security, limiting standalone CLI use. Microsoft Azure OpenAI, Mistral, and Groq all support standard OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code with PKCE for native/CLI apps, with Azure explicitly recommending this pattern via Entra ID and API Management; however, Azure OpenAI’s ToS and Azure-specific deployment constraints (e.g., VPC/perimeter requirements for managed endpoints) may necessitate service-keys or API-keys with scoped RBAC for unmanaged CLI use, making API keys with explicit resource-level permissions the most broadly usable fallback across providers.
sections.Synthesis:
The research reveals a fragmented and restrictive landscape for CLI agent authentication across major AI providers, with critical distinctions between OAuth suitability and API key viability that directly inform the design of Cercano’s setup wizard. For OpenAI, OAuth 2.0 is technically feasible via the Authorization Code flow with narrow scopes (`chat.completions`, `davinci`), but its practicality for an open-source CLI agent is severely undermined by ambiguous enforcement: hard, opaque rate limits (3,000 RPM / 1M TPM) trigger HTTP 429 errors without retry guidance or usage metrics—precisely the kind of invisible throttling that disrupts autonomous agent workflows. Moreover, while no explicit prohibition against third-party use of OAuth tokens exists in the archived ToS, the deprecation of Codex and lack of fine-tuning or file-access scopes signal that OpenAI intends OAuth to serve only interactive, user-facing applications—not long-running or programmatic agent sessions. Given these operational hazards, the cleanest path for Cercano’s wizard is to present API keys as the primary OpenAI option, supplemented with a clear warning about rate-limit unpredictability.

Google’s ecosystem presents a more infrastructure-focused but legally and technically constrained picture: while no dedicated CLI-agent OAuth flow exists for Gemini, VPC Service Controls demonstrate Google’s emphasis on perimeter-based security—making service account keys the dominant pattern for programmatic access. However, these keys are tied to VPC-network-bound perimeters, which block non-VPC traffic, including most CLI environments unless users meticulously configure firewall rules or enable private.googleapis.com access. This implies that, for a local-first CLI tool, API keys (not OAuth) remain the only reliable option for most users, though service account key rotation and VPC constraints must be clearly documented in the wizard to prevent misconfiguration. Microsoft and other providers like Mistral and Groq, by contrast, embrace gateway-centric architectures (e.g., Azure API Management with Entra ID), where OAuth 2.0 via Authorization Code + PKCE is not only supported but recommended—even for native or CLI clients—as long as the implementation adheres to modern security practices. Crucially, Microsoft’s own guidance mandates PKCE for all public clients and explicitly rejects less secure grants (like implicit or password-based), meaning Cercano’s wizard should prioritize OAuth with PKCE for providers offering it (e.g., Azure OpenAI), while defaulting to API keys where OAuth is either unavailable or operationally untenable (OpenAI, non-VPC-enabled Google services). Collectively, these findings indicate that no single provider offers a seamless, open-CLI-friendly OAuth experience: the wizard must tier options by reliability—OAuth-only where ToS explicitly permits and PKCE is enforced (Microsoft), API keys with warnings where throttling is punitive and opaque (OpenAI), and service-account caveats where network isolation is mandatory (Google).
sections.GapAnalysis:
Here are the **key gaps in the provided research findings**, specifically those that impact the user’s intent to design a robust, legally compliant, and technically feasible setup wizard for a **local-first CLI coding agent (Cercano)** targeting **OpenAI, Google, and other major providers**:

- **No evidence that OpenAI offers a consumer-account or subscription-based OAuth flow for CLI agents** — The findings mention `chat.completions`-limited OAuth, but no confirmation of public CLI-supporting OAuth (e.g., no mention of `offline_access`, `openid`, or device code grant flows), nor whether such flows work *without* a browser or GUI (critical for CLI agents).  
- **No analysis of OpenAI’s Terms of Service regarding third-party, open-source agent use of OAuth tokens or API keys** — Specifically absent:  
  - Clarification on whether client IDs registered via consumer accounts can be used by *unaffiliated, open-source tools* (e.g., redistribution, attribution, or TOS violation risks).  
  - Explicit prohibitions or permissions around CLI agents using OAuth tokens *programmatically* (e.g., silent token refresh in headless environments).  
- **No information on OpenAI’s stance on API-key rotation, token binding to IP/user-agent, or client-ID restrictions** — Critical for determining whether an open-source CLI agent can reliably use OAuth *or* API keys in diverse environments (e.g., Docker, CI, user’s laptop vs. server).  
- **No documentation or evidence of an official OpenAI “OAuth for headless/CLI” flow (e.g., Device Authorization Grant, RFC 8628)** — Despite its suitability for CLI tools, this is unmentioned entirely, even though it’s widely adopted by other providers (e.g., GitHub, Google).  
- **No specifics on Google’s OAuth availability for Gemini API in CLI contexts** — While Google OAuth 2.0 *generally* supports CLI flows (e.g., `gcloud auth login`, `device_code` grant), the research does **not confirm**:  
  - Whether the *Gemini API* (vs. general Google Cloud APIs) officially supports the Device Authorization Grant or similar headless flow.  
  - Whether ToS permits third-party tools (especially OSS) to implement such flows for end users.  
- **No evidence on whether Google’s client ID restrictions (e.g., for web vs. desktop app types) block open-source CLI agents** — Google often requires strict client ID registration with origin URLs; the research fails to assess how this applies to CLI agents (e.g., can a CLI use a “Desktop app”-type client ID without violating ToS?).  
- **No mention of legal restrictions (ToS, API Terms) on third-party use of Groq or Mistral APIs for CLI agents**, despite their inclusion in a finding — Only architectural patterns (e.g., API Management) are covered, not *authorization model* or *TOS permissiveness* for OSS.  
- **No data on supported OAuth flows for Mistral, Groq, or other non-major (but popular) providers** — The finding bundles them with Azure docs, but no details on whether *they* support CLI-friendly OAuth grants (e.g., device code), or if they only offer API keys.  
- **No data on OpenAI/Google/Groq/Mistral’s support for API keys with granular scopes or TTL-limited keys for CLI use cases** — Critical for design: the wizard needs to know if API-key alternatives should be offered, and what security trade-offs (e.g., over-permissioning) exist.  
- **No analysis of proxy compatibility (e.g., Meridian-style OAuth proxy) for providers other than Anthropic** — The research doesn’t evaluate whether OpenAI/Google OAuth tokens can be proxied or cached through a third-party service without violating ToS (e.g., token theft, scope creep).  
- **No mention of rate-limit visibility or fallback patterns for OAuth-based requests** — While OpenAI’s rate-limit opacity is covered for API keys, it’s unclear whether OAuth-based requests exhibit the *same* behavior (e.g., 429s without `Retry-After`), or if OAuth tokens have separate quota buckets (key for CLI UX).  

These gaps directly hinder the ability to:  
✅ Legally and safely suggest OAuth as a first-class option in the wizard  
✅ Decide when to fall back to API keys  
✅ Inform users about real-world constraints (e.g., “OAuth only works if you allow browser popups”)  
✅ Audit TOS compliance for open-source distribution  

Next steps should prioritize empirical testing (e.g., trying `device_code` flow with Gemini API) and direct legal review of provider ToS for *agent use cases*.

FollowUpQueries: Here are 3–5 high-impact, targeted follow-up research queries to close the critical gaps and directly inform Cercano’s setup wizard design:
**“OpenAI device authorization grant (RFC 8628) for chat.completions API in headless CLI — does it work? What scopes required?”**

— *Why*: Confirms whether OpenAI supports the only practical OAuth flow for CLI agents (no browser), and if so, which scopes (e.g., `openid`, `profile`, `offline_access`) are mandatory or supported — directly决定ing if a headless OAuth flow is technically viable.
**“OpenAI ToS §5 (Use Restrictions) and §3.3 (Sub-licensing) — does using a consumer OAuth client ID in an open-source CLI tool violate terms?”**

— *Why*: Resolves the legal risk of redistributing or embedding an open-source agent that uses OAuth tokens issued under personal consumer accounts — a make-or-break issue for Cercano’s distribution model.
**“Google Gemini API: Does the Device Authorization Grant (device_code) work with `gemini-api` OAuth scopes (e.g., `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/generative-language`)?”**

— *Why*: Google *does* support device flows broadly, but Gemini’s API may have scoped restrictions; verifying this empirically (e.g., via `curl` + `oauth2l`) eliminates guesswork and ensures CLI UX consistency.
**“Groq & Mistral: Do they support API keys with granular scopes (e.g., per-model or per-endpoint) or TTL-limited keys? What are their ToS clauses on open-source tooling?”**

— *Why*: These providers are popular but lack clarity on token hygiene and permissiveness for OSS — knowing if they offer scoped/TTL-limited keys (vs. monolithic keys) informs security guidance andwizard UX (e.g., “Use short-lived keys” vs. “Avoid API keys entirely”).
**“Can third-party OAuth proxies (e.g., Meridian-style) cache/forward Google/Anthropic/OpenAI tokens without violating ToS? Look for clauses on token storage, re-use, or ‘proxying’.”**

— *Why*: Enables Cercano to offer a unified, privacy-respecting auth pattern (like Anthropic’s Meridian) for *all* providers — but only if ToS permits token relaying/storage; this determines whether the wizard can unify OAuth flows or must provider-specific fallbacks.
